'''Ranjan Roy Daniel''' (also referred to as '''R. R. Daniel''' or '''Rajan Roy''') (11 August 1923&nbsp;– 27 March 2005) was an Indian physicist who worked in the fields of [[cosmic rays]] and [[space physics]],<ref name="insa" /> and remained Director Chairman of [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]].<ref name = "CS">Stephens, S. A. (10 October 2005), [http://www.iisc.ernet.in/currsci/oct102005/1277.pdf "Ranjan Roy Daniel (1923–2005)"], ''Current Science'', Vol. 89, No. 7, pp. 1277–1279, [[Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore]] IISC.</ref> He also served as an advisor to the prime minister of [[India]], [[Indira Gandhi]] in 1976. He worked in the field of cosmic rays<ref>Daniel, Ranjan Roy (ed.) (1964). [https://books.google.com/books?id=ZWH0NAEACAAJ ''Proceedings: Modulation'']{{Dead link|date=November 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}. International Union of Pure and Applied Physics. Cosmic Ray Commission, India. Dept. of Atomic Energy.</ref> with [[Homi Jehangir Bhabha]] for 23 years.

He was awarded the [[Padma Bhushan]] in 1992 by the [[Government of India]], for his contributions to science and engineering.<ref>{{cite web|title=Padma Awards Directory (1954–2009)|publisher=[[Ministry of Home Affairs (India)|Ministry of Home Affairs]]|url=http://www.mha.nic.in/pdfs/LST-PDAWD.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130510095705/http://www.mha.nic.in/pdfs/LST-PDAWD.pdf|archive-date=10 May 2013|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Daniel was born on 11 August 1923 in [[Nagercoil]] to M.A. Daniel Nadar and Theresa Chellammal Daniel. He was the third of five siblings. He received his early and secondary education at [[Scott Christian Higher Secondary School]] in his hometown, [[Nagercoil]]. After completing secondary school in 1939 from [[Scott Christian College]], he went on to pursue a BSc in physics from [[Loyola College, Chennai]], the [[University of Madras]].<ref name = "CS"/> Under the influence of the Indian Nobel laureate [[C. V. Raman|Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman]] he was advised to pursue the next phase of his education at [[Banaras Hindu University]], from which he received  MSc (Physics) degree in 1946.<ref name = "CS"/><ref name=tata>Ghosh, Swarna Kanti (February 2006). [http://www.tifr.res.in/~alumni/TAANL2006b.pdf "Remembering Prof. R.R. Daniel"]. ''Sampark'', Vol. 4 No. 1, pp. 9–10. Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.</ref>

==Career==
He joined [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]] (TIFR) in 1947 as a scientist.<ref name=josh/> From there he was sponsored by the Indian government to carry out research studies in the UK at the [[University of Bristol]] in 1951. He carried out research in the H. H. Wills Physics Laboratory, headed by the Nobel laureate [[C. F. Powell]], using nuclear emulsions exposed to cosmic rays at high altitudes. He completed his PhD research under [[Donald Hill Perkins]] in April 1953.<ref name = "CS"/><ref name=tata/> He went on to TIFR throughout till his retirement in 1988.

He was made a Fellow of the [[Indian National Science Academy]] (INSA) in 1975, and was awarded the Vainu Bappu Award in 1992.<ref name="insa">{{Cite web |url=http://insaindia.res.in/detail/N75-0179 |title=Deceased Fellow:Rajan Roy Daniel |publisher=[[Indian National Science Academy]] |access-date=4 February 2013 |archive-date=14 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114093514/http://insaindia.res.in/detail/N75-0179 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
He married Serena Padmini, second daughter of G.M. Samuel and Annammal Samuel, in 1948, and the couple had four children. After his retirement he returned to Nagercoil and lived in his daughter Lalitha's house. He was affectionately known as a simple man, and very few knew of his remarkable accomplishments.<ref name=josh>{{Cite web |url=http://joshfamily.com/362.html |title=Serena Padmini |access-date=4 February 2013 |archive-date=16 February 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130216073937/http://joshfamily.com/362.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> He died on 27 March 2005 after a prolonged illness.
He is survived by 4 children (Lalitha, Ravindran, Amudha and Renjitha) and several grandchildren, all of whom live in the USA and India.<ref name = "CS"/>
